stimulus.text: Land Ordinance of 1785 (May 20, 1785). Paraphrase: After the states ceded their western land claims to the national government, Congress ordered the land north of the Ohio River surveyed before it was sold or settled. Surveyors divided the land into townships six miles square. Each township held thirty-six sections of 640 acres. The ordinance reserved lot number 16 of every township “for the maintenance of public schools, within the said township.” It also reserved lots 8, 11, 26, and 29 for the United States. Land was sold at public auction at a minimum price of $1 an acre, and no buyer could buy less than one whole section (640 acres).
stimulus.source_note: Land Ordinance of May 20, 1785; the section 16 clause is quoted verbatim (public domain). Details from Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.7, and the Indiana Historical Bureau.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the Land Ordinance of May 20, 1785 (public domain).
stem: The survey system in the ordinance is best described as...

options.text: a set of grants along rivers, following the bends of the streams.
options.misconception: The ordinance used straight survey lines, not river bends, to mark townships.

options.text: a grid of square townships, each cut into numbered sections of 640 acres.
a free choice of land, with each settler marking whatever ground he cleared.
options.misconception: Settlers bought surveyed sections; they did not mark land by clearing it.

options.text: a lottery in which each family drew one section at random.
options.misconception: Land went by auction, not by lottery.

rationales.A: The lines ran due north-south and east-west, making squares, not river grants.
rationales.B: The ordinance ordered townships six miles square, each divided into thirty-six numbered sections of 640 acres.
rationales.C: The land was surveyed and numbered before sale; settlers bought sections, they did not claim by clearing.
rationales.D: Sections were sold at public auction, not drawn by lot.
rationales.general:
1. Surveyors ran straight lines north-south and east-west.
2. The lines made townships six miles square.
3. Each township was cut into 36 sections of 640 acres, numbered 1 to 36.
4. So the system was a grid, and a buyer could name a piece of land by its number.
Remember: a grid turns land into addresses: township, then section number.
